title.analysis: 'Do the Opposite' is an imperative curiosity gap; 'The Wealth Trick Rich People Use' adds status aspiration and suggests a concealed technique; the parenthetical names the mental model and restores search clarity. The actual promise is not literally to reverse every money decision. The script defines inversion as identifying behaviors that preserve poverty and avoiding them, then delivers an eleven-item mistake list. 'Rich people use' is broader than the evidence: Charlie Munger explicitly advocated inversion, but the stored text does not establish prevalence among wealthy people. The formulation is clear and script-aligned at the framework level but risks implying exclusivity and inevitability. Same-channel avoidance titles span 5.76468x STRONG (7W0uvrGuOW4, rich-tax strategy), 1.85513x TYPICAL (vS_FN5rpfis, Buffett mistakes), 0.89509x TYPICAL (LYPzhzZlsvg, post-$100K mistakes), 0.82458x TYPICAL (e06r3ZWyBVc, wealth killers), 0.65453x TYPICAL (dwbvvyeRonE, wealth killers), 0.49780x WEAK (NAg-Xx_xy8U, programmed to stay poor), 0.43388x WEAK (F9dpxZP8UXU, mistakes in your 20s), and 0.30109x WEAK (4vCP4Gxghb0, 401(k) mistakes). Avoidance/negative framing is therefore not a sufficient performance formula.

script.opening_words: Have you ever noticed that the smartest investors in the world seem to make money by doing the exact opposite of what everyone else is doing? While most people are chasing the latest get-rich-quick scheme or trying to time the perfect market entry, billionaires like
script.ending_words: wealth, you can build a fortune by simply not sabotaging yourself. Charlie Munger became a billionaire not by being the smartest guy in the room, but by consistently avoiding the obvious mistakes that destroy everyone else. Start there and let compound interest handle the rest.
script.analysis: The full 21,036-character canonical stored caption text was read in four contiguous ranges (0-6,000, 6,000-12,000, 12,000-18,000 and 18,000-21,036). The hook contrasts fashionable tactics with Munger/Buffett and reframes 'get rich' as 'do not stay poor'. A subscribe/like CTA arrives before the core teaching. The first act explains inversion through Jacobi and Munger, then uses a leaking-bucket analogy to move from principle to personal finance. Threat-avoidance and lottery-winner claims try to provide a psychological rationale. A Bezos regret-minimization story broadens the model from avoiding mistakes to avoiding future regret. The central payoff is an eleven-item anti-checklist: blaming income, revolving credit, lifestyle inflation, status purchases, no emergency fund, financial ignorance, perfectionist delay, unnecessary complexity, emotional decisions, harmful social norms, and extracting home equity for consumption. Repeated ordinal transitions make the long list easy to follow, but only the first ten receive full development; item eleven is introduced and then the script jumps immediately to the conclusion. The closing compresses the thesis into 'stop being stupid with money' and compound interest, without a final operational worksheet or prioritization. The strongest actionable material is the explicit failure-mode list. The weakest reasoning universalizes anecdotes and moralizes structural or emergency outcomes: external shocks are called excuses, income is said to have 'nothing' to do with wealth outcomes, lottery failure is asserted without a cited study, and social-circle prediction is presented with 'scary accuracy' but no measurement. Captions end abruptly after the conclusion; no spoken/audio completeness or editing claim is made.

claim_audit: SUPPORTED: Charlie Munger's 2007 USC address explicitly says problems often become easier when turned around, illustrates asking what does the worst damage and how to avoid it, and recommends asking what will fail. This supports the core inversion method. It does not establish that inversion itself created more millionaires than any other framework, that rich people generally use it, or that avoiding listed mistakes makes wealth inevitable.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: The script attributes 'invert, always invert' and the origin of the method to mathematician Carl Jacobi. Munger repeatedly popularized inversion and the Jacobi maxim is widely attributed, but the reviewed Munger speech transcript establishes inversion's use rather than a primary Jacobi document. The origin/wording remains secondary-source provenance in this audit.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: Berkshire's 2024 annual letter reports a 19.9% compounded annual gain in per-share market value for 1965-2024 versus 10.4% for the S&P 500 with dividends. That supports exceptional historical shareholder returns. It does not isolate 'simply avoiding mistakes' as the cause, and the script's 'thousands of shareholders wealthy' is not quantified.

UNVERIFIED: 'This one shift in perspective has created more millionaires than any other mental framework' is a comparative causal claim with no population, outcome definition or source in the stored text. 'Building wealth becomes almost inevitable' is likewise too strong; income, expenses, shocks, taxes, investment choice and returns still matter.

UNVERIFIED: 'Most lottery winners end up broke within a few years' is presented without a named dataset or study. No lottery population, jurisdiction, time horizon or definition of broke is supplied, so it is not used as evidence for inversion.

MISLEADING: 'The difference has nothing to do with how much money comes in' overstates the teacher/doctor anecdote. Spending, debt and behavior matter, but income directly affects feasible saving capacity. The examples are unsourced and cannot establish income irrelevance. The adjacent claim that every broke person has an excuse also collapses job loss, health, divorce and macro shocks into personal failure.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: The script's '20% annual interest' credit-card warning is realistic. The Federal Reserve's November 2025 report states average rates around 21.5% across all accounts and about 22.8% for accounts assessed interest at end-2024. But people who pay within the grace period do not incur finance charges, so card use and revolving high-interest debt should be distinguished.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: Prelec and Simester found higher willingness-to-pay in a credit-card condition for uncertain-value auction goods, but the effect was not always present; the second study's overall payment-method main effect was not significant and context mattered. The script's mechanistic statement that swiping removes pain and physical cash creates loss aversion is broader and more certain than this evidence.

SUPPORTED_WITH_ASSUMPTIONS: Investing $500 at each month-end for 30 years grows to about $609,986 at a nominal 7% annual rate compounded monthly, so 'over $600,000' reproduces near 7%. It is $180,000 with no return and about $745,180 at 8%. The script omits return, contribution timing, taxes, fees, inflation, volatility and interruption; it is a scenario, not the cost of every $500 car payment.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: IRS guidance confirms early retirement-plan or IRA withdrawals can be taxable and generally can face an additional 10% tax before age 59.5, subject to material exceptions; hardship distributions permanently reduce the plan balance. The script says one 'might' pay penalties and taxes, which is directionally sound, but account type, age and exception determine treatment.

SUPPORTED_WITH_ASSUMPTIONS: A person contributing $200 at each month-end from age 25 through 34 and then stopping can have more at 65 than someone contributing $200 monthly from 35 through 64, but only above roughly a 6.11% nominal annual return compounded monthly. At 7%, the modeled endpoints are about $280,968 versus $243,994; at 4%, the later saver has more ($138,810 versus $97,582). The script gives no return, fees, taxes, inflation or deposit-timing assumption, so presenting the outcome as automatic is misleading.

UNVERIFIED: 'Show me someone's five closest friends, and I can predict their financial future with scary accuracy' is not accompanied by a predictive study, measurement rule or accuracy rate. Munger's discussion of social-proof tendency supports the general possibility that peer behavior influences choices, not this quantitative-sounding prediction.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: The last item warns against repeatedly extracting home equity for consumption. That identifies leverage and housing-security risks, but the stored captions provide no rates, terms, loan-to-value, tax treatment or distinction between consumption, consolidation and productive uses. The abrupt transition prevents a full mechanism explanation.

topic.analysis: Evergreen personal-finance education that applies inversion thinking to controllable failure modes. Audience: people who feel standard 'save more/invest more' advice has not changed their position. The exact video uses inversion less as a decision tree than as a rhetorical wrapper for eleven familiar money mistakes. Mechanisms actually covered are spending leakage, revolving interest, fixed-cost ratcheting, opportunity cost, emergency liquidity, financial literacy, compounding delay, complexity, emotion, social proof and housing leverage. The useful distinction is between avoiding a preventable error and guaranteeing wealth; the script often crosses that boundary.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Create a genuine pre-mortem rather than another mistake list. Ask viewers to choose one planned decision, write the failure outcome, identify controllable causes, attach observable tripwires and pre-commit a response. A second experiment could rank the eleven failure modes by reversibility and expected cost, with a sourced calculator for credit-card interest and the two compound-growth examples. This keeps Munger's inversion method while replacing inevitability and moral blame with testable safeguards.
